name: STM32U575ZGT6
title: STM32U575xx ultra-low-power Arm Cortex-M33 microcontrollers with TrustZone and FPU, 160 MHz, 1 or 2 Mbytes flash, 786 Kbytes SRAM, 1.71 V to 3.6 V
summary: An ultra-low-power Cortex-M33 microcontroller line with TrustZone, FPU, DSP instructions and an MPU, running at up to 160 MHz from 1.71 V to 3.6 V, with 1 or 2 Mbytes of dual-bank ECC flash, 786 Kbytes of SRAM, an internal LDO and an SMPS step-down converter. It carries a 14-bit and a 12-bit 2.5 Msps ADC, two 12-bit DACs, two op amps, two comparators, USB OTG full speed, a USB Type-C Power Delivery controller, FDCAN, two Octo-SPI interfaces, an FSMC on larger packages, up to 17 timers and a large set of serial interfaces, in eight packages from 48 to 169 pins. STM32U575ZGT6 is the 1-Mbyte LQFP144 part without the SMPS pinout, for -40 °C to 85 °C ambient, with 114 GPIOs.
key_figures: Arm Cortex-M33 with TrustZone, MPU, DSP and FPU, up to 160 MHz, 240 DMIPS
1 or 2 Mbytes flash with ECC in two banks; 786 Kbytes SRAM (722 Kbytes with up to 322 Kbytes under ECC)
1.71 V to 3.6 V; LDO and SMPS step-down converter
4.0 µA / 1.9 µA with 16 Kbytes SRAM kept; 8.95 µA / 4.3 µA with all SRAM
210 nA (530 nA with RTC) / 160 nA, 24 wake-up pins
14-bit 2.5 Msps and 12-bit 2.5 Msps (the 12-bit one autonomous in Stop 2), hardware oversampling
two 12-bit DACs, two op amps with PGA, two ultra-low-power comparators
OTG 2.0 full speed; USB Type-C / Power Delivery controller
114 GPIOs without SMPS, 111 with; most 5 V tolerant; up to 14 I/Os supplied down to 1.08 V
4 to 50 MHz crystal, 32 kHz crystal, HSI16 ±1%, LSI 32 kHz ±5%, two MSI 100 kHz to 48 MHz, HSI48, three PLLs
-40 °C to 85 °C or 125 °C ambient (105 °C or 130 °C junction) by order code

pins.name: PC13
pins.function: FT I/O. Alternate functions: EVENTOUT. Additional functions: RTC_TS/RTC_OUT1, TAMP_IN1/TAMP_OUT2, WKUP2. Supplied through the backup power switch (VSW), which sinks at most 3 mA: as an output it runs at 2 MHz or less into 30 pF or less and must never source current, such as into an LED. notes: (1) With Level 2 active, the debug port, boot from RAM and boot from system memory are all disabled.
(2) System memory can only be read, at every protection level and in every execution mode.
(3) Option bytes are reached only through the flash memory registers and the OPSTRT bit.

(5) The SWAP_BANK option bit can still be changed.
(6) The OTP area can be written once only.
(7) Changing RDP from Level 1 to Level 0 erases the backup registers.
(8) Changing RDP from Level 1 to Level 0 erases all SRAMs.

notes: (1) LPR: main regulator off, low-power regulator on.
(2) Every peripheral can be active or have its clock gated to save power.
(3) When code runs from SRAM the flash can be powered down with its clock gated; one bank alone can also be powered down.
(4) The clocks of SRAM1, SRAM2, SRAM3, SRAM4 and BKPSRAM are gated on or off independently.
(5) Each SRAM can be powered off on its own to save power.
(6) MSI and HSI16 can be turned on for a while at a peripheral's request, for autonomous work with DMA or for wake-up event detection in Stop.
(7) ADC4 converts autonomously with DMA in Stop mode and can raise a wake-up interrupt on conversion events.
(8) DAC1 is the controller instance driving two D/A converters (two channels); its conversions run autonomously with DMA in Stop mode.
(9) U(S)ART and LPUART send and receive autonomously with DMA in Stop mode and can raise a wake-up interrupt on transfer events.
(10) SPI sends and receives autonomously with DMA in Stop mode and can raise a wake-up interrupt on transfer events.
(11) I2C sends and receives autonomously with DMA in Stop mode and can raise a wake-up interrupt on transfer events.
(12) LPTIM runs autonomously with DMA in Stop mode and can raise a wake-up interrupt on all events.
(13) MDF and ADF run autonomously with DMA in Stop mode and can raise a wake-up interrupt on events.
(14) GPDMA and LPDMA run autonomously in Stop mode and can raise a wake-up interrupt on events.
(15) Pull-up, pull-down or floating can be set for the I/Os in Shutdown, and the setting is lost on leaving Shutdown.

tables.title: Functions available in each mode (1)
rows: Backup domain voltage and temperature monitoring
notes: (1) Y: enabled. O: optional, off by default and turned on by software. -: not available.
(2) The flash can be put in power-down mode; it is not by default.
(3) Each SRAM is powered on or off independently.
(4) Each SRAM clock is gated on or off independently.
(5) Wake-up from Stop by an ECC error interrupt or NMI.
(6) 8 Kbytes, 56 Kbytes or all of SRAM2 can be kept.

(7) To save power, sub-blocks or all of SRAM1 and SRAM3, all of SRAM2, and SRAM4 can be switched off. GPDMA1 reaches SRAM1 to SRAM4 in Stop 0 and Stop 1; LPDMA1 reaches SRAM4 in Stop 0, Stop 1 and Stop 2.
(8) GPDMA transfers run autonomously in Stop mode and raise a wake-up interrupt on transfer events.
(9) LPDMA transfers run autonomously in Stop mode and raise a wake-up interrupt on transfer events.
(10) An autonomous peripheral able to wake the part from Stop can ask for HSI16, MSIS or MSIK; the oscillator then starts for it and turns off again once no peripheral needs it.
(11) OTG_FS works in voltage scaling Range 1, 2 and 3.
(12) USART and LPUART send and receive autonomously in Stop mode in asynchronous and SPI master modes, and raise a wake-up interrupt on transfer events.
(13) I2C sends and receives autonomously in Stop mode and raises a wake-up interrupt on transfer events.
(14) SPI sends and receives autonomously in Stop mode and raises a wake-up interrupt on transfer events.
(15) A/D conversion runs autonomously in Stop mode and raises a wake-up interrupt on conversion events.
(16) LPTIM runs autonomously in Stop mode and raises a wake-up interrupt on events.
(17) Only an IWDG reset brings the part out of Stop 3 or Standby; an IWDG interrupt does not wake it.
(18) MDF and ADF run autonomously in Stop mode and raise a wake-up interrupt on events.
(19) In Stop 3 and Standby each I/O can be left floating or given its internal pull-up or pull-down.
(20) In Shutdown each I/O can be left floating or given its internal pull-up or pull-down; the setting is lost on leaving Shutdown.

(2) An I/O structure name stands for every structure that includes it: TT_a covers any TT I/O with the _a option, TT_xx any TT I/O and FT_xx any FT I/O.

notes: (1) Every main power pin (VDD, VDDSMPS, VDDA, VDDUSB, VDDIO2, VBAT) and ground pin (VSS, VSSA, VSSSMPS) is always connected to its external supplies, within the permitted range.
(2) The total is spread over all I/Os and control pins; on high pin-count QFP packages it is not all sunk or sourced between two neighbouring supply pins.
(3) These I/Os take no positive injection (VIN > VDDIOx), and none occurs at inputs below the specified maximum voltage.

circuits.title: Power supply scheme without SMPS

VDD takes a 100 nF capacitor at each VDD pin plus one 10 µF; VDDIO2 a 100 nF at each VDDIO2 pin plus one 4.7 µF; VDDA 100 nF + 1 µF; VREF+ 100 nF + 1 µF to VSSA; VDDUSB 100 nF. VCAP, the LDO output for VCORE, takes 4.7 µF. A 1.65 V to 3.6 V source on VBAT keeps the backup domain (LSE, RTC, TAMP, backup registers, backup SRAM) running through the internal power switch.
notes: Every VDD, VDDIO2 and VSS pin is connected; C3 and C5 stand for one capacitor per pin.

circuits.title: Power supply scheme with SMPS
circuits.description: Decoupling on an SMPS part (xQ order codes). VDDSMPS joins VDD with a 10 µF input capacitor; a 2.2 µH inductor runs from VLXSMPS to the two VDD11 pins, which carry 2 × 2.2 µF to VSSSMPS and receive VCORE from the SMPS, or hold it when the LDO is running instead. VDD, VDDIO2, VDDA, VREF+ and VDDUSB are decoupled as on the parts without SMPS, and a 1.65 V to 3.6 V source on VBAT keeps the backup domain running.
notes: Every VDD, VDDIO2, VDD11 and VSS pin is connected; C3 and C5 stand for one capacitor per pin.
A 100 nF capacitor at each VDD11 pin is advised but optional.

Inductor: 2.2 µH ±20 %, saturation current above 0.5 A, DC resistance under 200 mΩ. VDD11 capacitors: ±20 %, ESR under 20 mΩ at 3 MHz, rated 10 V or more. VDDSMPS capacitor: ±20 %, ESR under 10 mΩ at 3 MHz, rated 10 V or more.

operation.text: Benchmarks: 1.5 DMIPS/MHz (Dhrystone 2.1), 651 CoreMark (4.07 CoreMark/MHz), 450 ULPMark-CP, 109 ULPMark-PP, 51.5 ULPMark-CM, 133000 SecureMark-TLS. Low-power figures: Shutdown 160 nA and Standby 210 nA with 24 wake-up pins, Standby with RTC 530 nA, Stop 3 1.9 µA with 16 Kbytes of SRAM retained or 4.3 µA with all of it, Stop 2 4.0 µA or 8.95 µA on the same terms, Run 19.5 µA/MHz at 3.3 V. The 8-Kbyte instruction cache gives zero-wait-state execution from flash and external memory up to 160 MHz (240 DMIPS); a 4-Kbyte data cache serves external memory. 512 Kbytes of the 2-Mbyte flash are rated for 100 kcycles; flash is read-while-write across its two banks. A 512-byte OTP area and a 96-bit unique ID are fitted.

As many as 136 fast I/Os, each able to raise an interrupt, most of them 5 V tolerant. Timers: two 16-bit advanced motor-control, four 32-bit and five 16-bit general purpose and basic, four 16-bit low-power timers that keep running in Stop, two SysTick timers, two watchdogs, and a calendar RTC with calibration. Communication: USB OTG 2.0 full speed, USB Type-C/PD, two SAIs, four I2Cs (Fm+ 1 Mbit/s, SMBus/PMBus), six USARTs (ISO 7816, LIN, IrDA, modem), three SPIs (five counting the two OCTOSPIs), one CAN FD, two SDMMCs, an MDF with six filters and an ADF with sound-activity detection, a parallel synchronous slave interface (PSSI) and a camera interface. DMA: a 16-channel and a 4-channel controller, working in Stop. Also a Chrom-ART (DMA2D) graphics accelerator, CORDIC and FMAC maths accelerators, up to 22 capacitive sensing channels, a CRC unit, and SWD, JTAG and ETM debug. Security: TrustZone with securable I/Os, memories and peripherals, RDP levels with password-protected debug, a unique boot entry and hide protection area (HDP), secure firmware install through root secure services (RSS), TF-M firmware upgrade, HASH accelerator, a true random number generator (NIST SP800-90B) and active tampers. Packages are ECOPACK2.

The single-precision FPU handles every Arm single-precision instruction and data type. The FSMC for static memories exists only on packages of 90 pins or more, and at least one Quad-SPI port is available on every package. Peripherals hang off three APB and three AHB buses through a 32-bit multi-AHB bus matrix. Flash and SRAM can be guarded by readout protection, write protection, secure areas and hide protection areas. The security set complies with the Arm TBSA requirements: secure boot, secure storage, secure update and secure provisioning of code in production, with privilege control on peripherals and memories. Its security peripherals bring DPA resistance, and on an attack detected by the internal monitors, secret data is erased.

The devices work from 1.71 V to 3.6 V over -40 °C to +85 °C ambient (+105 °C junction) or -40 °C to +125 °C (+130 °C junction). VDDA is a separate supply for the ADCs, DACs, op amps and comparators; VDDUSB is a dedicated 3.3 V supply for the USB; VDDIO2 supplies up to 14 I/Os down to 1.08 V; VBAT, from a backup battery, keeps the RTC, the 32 backup registers of 32 bits and the 2-Kbyte backup SRAM. Many communication, analog, timer and audio peripherals keep working with DMA down to Stop mode through LPBAM.

Arm Cortex-M33 implementing the Armv8-M main extension with TrustZone (secure and nonsecure states), a single-precision FPU and DSP instructions. Memory protection units give up to 16 regions for each of the secure and nonsecure sides, and the SAU marks up to eight regions secure or nonsecure. Instruction fetches and data accesses to the code region go over the C-AHB bus; those to SRAM, peripherals, external RAM and devices and the Vendor_SYS region go over the S-AHB system bus.

Sits on the C-AHB code bus and caches fetches from internal and external memory. It has two master ports, one refilling from flash and SRAM, the other from external memory behind the Octo-SPI and FMC interfaces, so slow external traffic stays off the fast bus. A hit costs no wait state; a miss is refilled critical word first with AHB bursts of one line while later hits are still served. It is two-way set-associative with a binary-tree pseudo-LRU replacement, or direct mapped for lower power. Four external regions can be remapped as cacheable. It has hit and miss counters, TrustZone support, maintenance operations for coherency, and flags an unexpected cacheable write, optionally with an interrupt.

Sits on the S-AHB system bus and caches data traffic to external memory (Octo-SPI and FMC). No wait state on a hit, hit-under-miss, critical-word-first refill on reads, two-way set-associative with pseudo-LRU replacement, burst refill of one line, and separate read and write hit and miss counters. Write-back or write-through is chosen per access by the AHB bufferable attribute; reads and write-backs allocate, write-through does not. Byte, half-word and word writes are accepted. Full invalidation (not interruptible) and background clean or invalidate of an address range (interruptible) keep it coherent; an error on a line eviction or clean can raise an interrupt.

The MPU divides memory into up to 16 protected areas so one task cannot corrupt the memory or resources of another; its regions and registers are banked between the secure and nonsecure states. An access the MPU forbids is detected so an RTOS can act, and the kernel can change the areas for each process. Applications that do not need it can leave it bypassed.

Up to 2 Mbytes of flash for code and data, rated for 10 000 cycles, and 100 000 cycles on 512 Kbytes. A 128-bit instruction prefetch can be enabled. The flash is dual-bank with read-while-write: one bank is read while the other is erased or programmed, and boot from either bank is supported. Each bank holds 128 pages of 8 Kbytes. There are 512 bytes of one-time-programmable memory for user data. The whole nonvolatile memory has ECC that corrects single errors, detects double errors and reports the address that failed.

Option bytes set the protections. Write protection guards up to two areas per bank, in 8-Kbyte steps, against erase and programming. Readout protection (RDP) has four levels. Level 0: none. Level 0.5 (only with TrustZone enabled): the nonsecure flash can be read and written, debug of the secure area is blocked and debug of the nonsecure area still works. Level 1: the flash cannot be read or written while a debugger is connected or when booting from RAM or the bootloader; with TrustZone enabled nonsecure debug still works and boot from SRAM is not possible; going back to a lower level can be guarded by a password. Level 2: debug, boot from RAM and the bootloader are disabled; it is permanent and JTAG/SWD stays off unless a secret key was set in the secure options at a lower level, in which case a password given over JTAG/SWD returns the part to Level 1. The highest protection level is TrustZone enabled together with RDP Level 2 and password-authenticated regression.

With TrustZone enabled in the option bytes, all of the flash is secure after reset. Per bank there is one nonvolatile watermark-defined secure area, set with page granularity and reachable only in secure mode, and at its start one secure hide-protection area (HDP): code there can run once and then be shut off from all reads, writes and fetches until the next system reset. Any page can also be made secure or nonsecure on the fly (volatile block-based secure area), and any page can be made privileged or unprivileged on the fly.

With TrustZone enabled all SRAMs are secure after reset. SRAM1 to SRAM4 are made secure or nonsecure, and privileged or unprivileged, in pages of 512 bytes by the block-based memory protection controller (MPCBB). Backup SRAM regions are set the same way by watermark through the TZSC in the GTZC.

TrustZone is turned on by the TZEN option bit in FLASH_OPTR. The SAU (up to eight configurable regions) and the IDAU then decide the security of each address; the IDAU gives a first nonsecure or nonsecure-callable split, it is combined with the SAU result and the more secure of the two applies. Flash, system SRAM and the peripheral space appear twice in the memory map, once for each state; external memory space is not aliased.

A peripheral is either securable (behind an AHB/APB firewall gate whose security is set from the TZSC) or TrustZone-aware (on the bus directly, with its own secure behaviour such as some secure registers). After reset: the Cortex-M33 is in the secure state and must boot from a secure address; the SAU is fully secure, so the whole memory map is; the flash secure area is set by the watermark user options and the block-based flash area is nonsecure; all SRAMs and the MPCBB are secure; the FSMC and OCTOSPI banks and the MPCWMx are secure; securable and TrustZone-aware peripherals are nonsecure, with the secure configuration registers of the latter secure; all GPIOs are secure; all NVIC interrupts are secure, the NVIC being banked; all TZIC illegal-access interrupts are disabled.

At start-up the BOOT0 pin, the nBOOT0 option bit and the NSBOOTADDx[24:0] (x = 0, 1) and SECBOOTADD0[24:0] option bytes choose the boot address: anywhere in user flash, the system-memory bootloader, anywhere in embedded SRAM, or the root security services (RSS). BOOT0 is taken from the PH3-BOOT0 pin or, when a user option bit frees that pad, from an option bit. The factory bootloader in system memory, present on every device, reprograms the flash over USART, I2C, SPI, FDCAN or USB FS device (DFU). The RSS sit in the secure information block of flash, programmed by ST; they provide secure firmware installation (SFI) through the RSSe SFI extension, keeping firmware confidential when production is done by a third party, and are available once TrustZone is enabled. With TrustZone enabled the boot address must be secure and is set by SECBOOTADD0[24:0]; setting BOOT_LOCK makes that the only boot entry and all other boot options are ignored.

The GTZC sets TrustZone and privilege attributes across the system through three blocks, each with its own 32-bit AHB interface. The TZSC sets the secure and privileged state of slave and master peripherals and the nonsecure area sizes of the watermark memory controllers (MPCWM), and tells the RCC and GPIO logic which securable peripherals are secure. The TZIC collects every illegal security access and raises a secure interrupt to the NVIC. The MPCBB sets the security and privilege of each 512-byte page of SRAM. Registers set secure and privileged regions for external memories and the access mode of securable peripherals and legacy masters.

Supply domains: VCORE, VDD, backup (VBAT), analog (VDDA), the SMPS power stage (VDDSMPS, SMPS packages only), VDDIO2 and VDDUSB for the USB transceiver. The core supply comes from an SMPS step-down converter or an LDO. Supervision: BOR, PVD, and PVM on VDDA, VDDUSB and VDDIO2. It also handles operating and low-power modes, voltage scaling, VBAT battery charging and TrustZone and privilege protection.

An LDO and an SMPS work in parallel to supply VCORE to the digital peripherals, SRAM1 to SRAM4 and the flash. The SMPS output is on the two VDD11 pins with 4.7 µF typical in total and needs an external 2.2 µH typical inductor; the LDO output is on VCAP with an external 4.7 µF typical capacitor. Both give four voltages (voltage scaling), both run in Stop modes, and the part can switch between them on the fly.

VDDA feeds the ADCs, comparators, DACs, op amps and reference buffer. VDDUSB feeds the USB transceiver. VDDIO2 feeds the I/O ring of PG[15:2]. VDD feeds the VDDIO1 I/O ring, the reset block, temperature sensor, three PLLs, internal RC oscillators, the standby circuitry (wake-up logic, IWDG), the regulators and a low-voltage detector. VCORE feeds the core, SRAM1 to SRAM4, the digital peripherals and the flash. The backup domain, fed through the VSW switch, holds the LSE and LSI oscillators, backup registers, RCC_BDCR and PWR_BDCR1, RTC, TAMP and BKPSRAM. VSW is VDD while VDD is above VBOR0 and VBAT below it. VDDIO1 comes from VDD.

While VDD is below 1 V, VDDA, VDDIO2 and VDDUSB must stay below VDD + 300 mV. Above 1 V all supplies are independent. During power-down VDD may briefly fall below the other supplies provided the energy delivered to the MCU stays under 1 mJ, so decoupling capacitors may discharge at different rates.

An ultra-low-power BOR, active in every mode except Shutdown, holds the part in reset while VDD is below threshold, so no external reset circuit is needed. At power-on the BOR threshold is 1.71 V at its lowest; option bytes select higher ones. A software-enabled PVD compares VDD with VPVD and can interrupt as VDD falls below and/or rises above it. A peripheral voltage monitor checks that VDDA, VDDUSB and VDDIO2 are within their working ranges.

Run follows any system or power reset. Sleep stops only the CPU; peripherals keep running and an interrupt or event wakes it. Stop 0 to Stop 3 keep SRAM and register contents; SRAMs can be switched off wholly or in part. All VCORE-domain clocks stop and the PLL, MSI, HSI16, HSI48 and HSE are off; LSE or LSI keeps running and the RTC may stay on. Autonomous peripherals request their kernel clock and bus when needed and move data by DMA: GPDMA1 in Stop 0 and Stop 1, LPDMA1 in Stop 0, Stop 1 and Stop 2. LPBAM is not available in Stop 3. In Stop 2 and Stop 3 most of the VCORE domain goes into a lower-leakage state. Stop 0 and Stop 1 have the most active peripherals and wake-up sources and wake faster than Stop 2, at higher consumption; in Stop 0 the main regulator stays on, giving the fastest wake-up at much higher consumption. Stop 3 keeps everything at the least power of any retaining mode, with only the peripherals and wake-up sources of Standby. On leaving Stop 0, 1 or 2 the system clock is MSI up to 24 MHz or HSI16, as configured.

The lowest-power mode that keeps the BOR. The regulator is off, so the VCORE domain loses power, and the PLL, MSI, HSI16, HSI48 and HSE are off; the RTC may stay on and the BOR is always on (it can be put in an ultra-low-power mode). Each I/O can be held with pull-up, pull-down or floating. SRAM and register contents are lost except the backup domain registers, backup SRAM and the standby circuitry; the whole of SRAM2, or 8 Kbytes or 56 Kbytes of it, can be kept powered by the low-power regulator. Exit is by NRST, an IWDG reset, a WKUP pin edge (rising or falling, selectable), an RTC alarm, periodic wake-up or timestamp, or a tamper event from a pin or an internal failure detector. On wake-up the part runs from MSI at up to 4 MHz.

The lowest consumption. The regulator is off and the PLL, HSI16, HSI48, MSI, LSI and HSE are off; the RTC may stay on. There is no BOR and no supply monitoring, so the switch to the backup domain (VBAT mode) is not supported. SRAM and register contents are lost except the backup domain registers while VDD is present. Exit is by NRST, a WKUP pin edge (rising or falling, selectable), an RTC alarm, periodic wake-up or timestamp, or a tamper event. On wake-up the part runs from MSI at 4 MHz.

Peripherals keep working with no software running in Stop 0, Stop 1 and Stop 2. In Stop 0 and Stop 1 the autonomous peripherals are ADC4, DAC1, LPTIM1 to LPTIM4, USART1 to USART5, LPUART1, SPI1 to SPI3, I2C1 to I2C4, MDF1, ADF1, GPDMA1 and LPDMA1; GPDMA1 reaches SRAM1 to SRAM4 and LPDMA1 reaches SRAM4. In Stop 2 they are ADC4, DAC1, LPTIM1, LPTIM3, LPTIM4, LPUART1, SPI3, I2C3, ADF1 and LPDMA1, with LPDMA1 reaching SRAM4. Each such peripheral switches its own kernel clock on when it needs it and off after; a request for the system clock (MSI or HSI16) wakes it and distributes it to every peripheral enabled in the RCC, so DMA can reach enabled SRAM and peripheral registers such as GPIO or LPGPIO. Peripherals start on hardware triggers (I/O edges, low-power timer events) and can wake the part with an interrupt. GPDMA and LPDMA update their linked lists in Stop, chaining transfers or rewriting peripheral registers without waking the CPU; memory-to-memory transfers can be started, and peripheral transfers gated, by hardware triggers. Uses in Stop include timer-triggered A/D or D/A conversion with wake-up on an analog-watchdog or DMA-buffer event; audio filter data to SRAM with wake-up on sound activity; I2C slave, SPI receive and UART/LPUART receive with wake-up at the end of transfer; timer-triggered I2C master, SPI transmit and UART/LPUART transmit (periodic sensor reads); passing ADC data to a communication peripheral; and GPIO/LPGPIO to or from SRAM to drive external parts or carry a protocol.
Under and after reset the I/Os are in analog state with the Schmitt trigger off, to cut consumption, and the internal pull-up on NRST is disconnected when the reset comes from inside the part.

VBAT, from a battery or supercapacitor, powers the RTC with the LSE, the antitamper logic (TAMP) with its eight tamper pins, the backup registers and the 2-Kbyte backup SRAM. The part changes to VBAT supply by itself when VDD is absent. A VBAT charging circuit inside can be enabled while VDD is present. Running from VBAT, neither external interrupts nor RTC or TAMP alarms and events take the part out of VBAT operation.

With TZEN set, the PWR secures the low-power mode, wake-up pin, voltage detection and monitoring and VBAT mode settings. The voltage scaling setting follows the security of the RCC system clock selection, and the Standby pull-up/pull-down setting of an I/O is secure when that GPIO is secure.

Some peripherals are wired directly to one another so they can work together without the CPU, saving power, with fast and predictable latency. Depending on the peripherals these links work in Run, Sleep, Stop 0, Stop 1 and Stop 2.

The RCC handles the reset types and makes every bus and peripheral clock, with programmable prescalers, clock gating of the core, peripherals and memory, and safe on-the-fly change of clock source in Run. SYSCLK comes from one of four sources: HSE (4 to 50 MHz crystal or ceramic resonator, or an external clock in bypass), HSI16 (16 MHz RC, software-trimmed), MSI (RC, software-trimmed, 16 frequencies from 100 kHz to 48 MHz; with the LSE present it can be trimmed by hardware to better than ±0.25 %, enough to clock the USB device with no HSE), or the system PLL (from HSE, HSI16 or MSI, up to 160 MHz). HSI48, a 48 MHz RC with the clock recovery system, can clock the USB, SDMMC or RNG and can be sent to MCO. The UCPD kernel clock comes from HSI16, which must be on first. The RTC can run from the LSE (32.768 kHz crystal, three drive levels, or bypass) or the LSI (32 kHz RC, ±5 %, also the IWDG clock; it can be divided by 128 to give 250 Hz). Three PLLs with three outputs each give independent kernel clocks to the SAIs, OCTOSPIs, FDCAN1, ADF, MDF, RNG, SDMMC, USB and ADC. After reset the part runs from MSI. The clock security system, enabled by software, moves the system clock to HSI16 on an HSE failure with an optional interrupt, and also detects an LSE failure with an interrupt. MCO puts an internal clock on a pin; LSCO outputs LSI or LSE in every low-power mode except VBAT. The AHB and APB domains run at up to 160 MHz.

With TZEN set the RCC enters TrustZone mode: for a secure peripheral its clock, reset, clock source selection and low-power clock enable bits are secure and hidden from nonsecure access. A securable peripheral is secure when its SEC bit is set in the TZSC; a TrustZone-aware one when its own security feature is enabled.

Trims the internal 48 MHz oscillator automatically over the whole operating range from a synchronization signal: the USB SOF, the LSE, an external signal on CRS_SYNC, or software. Automatic and manual trimming can be combined to lock faster at start-up.

Each GPIO can be an output (push-pull or open-drain), an input (floating, pull-up or pull-down) or an alternate function; most carry shared digital or analog alternate functions. Reset leaves every GPIO in analog mode, which saves power. The alternate-function configuration can be locked by a set sequence against stray writes. Each pin can be made secure, which restricts its alternate function, mode and data bits to secure software; after reset all GPIO ports are secure.
Lets LPDMA1 drive up to 16 I/Os in Stop 2, each an input or an output (open-drain or push-pull as set in the GPIO). An LPGPIO bit is secure when its I/O is secure in the GPIO.

A 32-bit multi-AHB bus matrix joins the masters (CPU, DMA2D, GPDMA1, SDMMC1, SDMMC2) to the slaves (flash, RAM, FMC, OCTOSPIs, SRAMs, AHB and APB) so several fast peripherals can work at once. A second matrix joins two masters, a slave port of the first matrix and LPDMA1, to the slaves that work in Stop 2: SRAM4 and the AHB/APB peripherals that run in Stop 2.
Registers for the robustness features, FPU interrupts, the Fm+ high drive on certain I/Os and the voltage booster of the I/O analog switches, the I/O compensation cell, and register security access.

A bus master with two bidirectional AHB master ports, moving data between any mix of memories and peripherals in either direction, from linked lists, also in Sleep and Stop. 16 concurrent channels, each with a FIFO; arbitration by four programmed priorities, one high-priority class for time-critical channels (queue 3) and three low-priority classes shared by weighted round-robin (queues 0, 1, 2). Each channel raises events and separately enabled interrupts on transfer complete, half transfer, transfer error, user setting error, linked-list update error or completed suspension. Transfers chain inside a channel through a linked list in memory (run-to-completion or link-step mode) and between channels through DMA input triggers. Per linked-list item: separate source and destination, byte reordering, packing and unpacking, padding and truncation, sign extension, left or right alignment, block size in bytes, request and trigger selection, half and complete events, and a pointer to the next item. Twelve channels address linearly (fixed or incrementing); four have 2D addressing with signed offsets between bursts and between blocks, for scatter-gather and interleaving. Channels can be suspended and resumed and report FIFO level and flags. Transfers are secure or nonsecure per channel and per source/destination and link, and privileged or unprivileged per channel; the slave port is TrustZone- and privilege-aware.

As the GPDMA but with one bidirectional AHB master port and four concurrent channels, all with linear addressing (fixed or incrementing) and no FIFO, and data handling limited to padding or truncation, sign extension and left or right alignment. It has the same four-grade priority arbitration, per-channel events and interrupts, linked-list and trigger chaining, suspend and resume, status reporting, and TrustZone and privilege support.

A DMA for images: fills an area with one colour, copies an area, copies with colour-format conversion, and blends two sources of different formats into a destination of another format. Eleven colour formats of 4 to 32 bits per image element, indexed or direct, with two internal CLUT memories loaded automatically or by the CPU, of programmable size. One AHB master; AHB slave registers accessed in 8, 16 or 32 bits (CLUT in 32 bits only). Programmable area size, source and destination addresses anywhere in memory, offsets counted in image elements or bytes, alpha taken from the source, fixed or modulated, and an internal timer that caps its AHB bandwidth. Its six operating modes: fill from a register; plain copy between memories; copy with format conversion; conversion with blending; and conversion with blending against either a fixed foreground or a fixed background colour. Output byte swapping for refreshing displays over a parallel interface; abort and suspend; interrupts on a programmable destination line (watermark), bus error or access conflict, and completion.

16 priority levels and as many as 125 maskable interrupt channels, besides the 16 Cortex-M33 interrupt lines. Closely coupled for low latency: the vector address goes straight to the core, late-arriving higher-priority interrupts are handled, tail-chaining is supported and processor state is saved and restored by hardware with no instruction overhead. Its registers are banked for the secure and nonsecure states.

Gives wake-up requests to the power controller, interrupts to the NVIC and events to the CPU (through an event generator), from configurable inputs; its wake-ups bring the part out of Stop, and interrupts and events also work in Run. Every input can wake the part. Each configurable input has a selectable edge, separate pending bits for rising and falling edges, separate interrupt and event masks, and a software trigger. Control of secure inputs can be made secure. It includes the I/O port selection multiplexer.

Computes a CRC with a configurable polynomial and size, for checking transmitted or stored data. Under EN/IEC 60335-1 it can check the flash at run time against a signature computed at link time and stored in memory.

Hardware for trigonometric and related functions: a 24-bit CORDIC engine in circular and hyperbolic modes, rotation and vectoring, computing sin, cos, sinh, cosh, atan, atan2, atanh, modulus, square root and ln at programmable precision. A result can be read the moment it is ready, with no polling or interrupt, over a low-latency AHB slave port, with DMA read and write channels and multiple register access by DMA.

A multiply-accumulate unit with address generation over a local memory, for FIR and IIR (direct form 1) filters and vector dot product, convolution and correlation. 16 x 16-bit multiplier, 24 + 2-bit accumulator with add and subtract, 16-bit input and output, 256 x 16-bit local memory holding up to three buffers (two inputs, one output) with programmable base and size, which can be circular. AHB slave with DMA read and write channels.

Also called FMC. A NOR/PSRAM controller and a NAND controller for SRAM, NOR and OneNAND flash, PSRAM (four banks), NAND flash with hardware ECC over up to 8 Kbytes of data, and FRAM. 8- or 16-bit data bus, a chip select and configuration per bank, and a write FIFO. It can drive graphic LCD controllers in Intel 8080 or Motorola 6800 mode. With TrustZone enabled all FSMC banks are secure after reset: up to two nonsecure areas of the NOR/PSRAM bank are set through the TZSC MPCWM2 in 64-Kbyte steps, the NAND bank is made wholly secure or wholly nonsecure through MPCWM3, and the FSMC registers can be made secure through the TZSC.

Two OCTOSPIs for serial PSRAM, serial NAND and NOR flash, HyperRAM and HyperFlash. Modes: indirect (through registers), status polling (reads the memory status register and interrupts on a flag) and memory-mapped (read and write, the memory seen as internal). Standard frames (command, address, alternate bytes, dummy cycles, data) or HyperBus frames; single, dual, quad and octal lines, and dual-quad (two quad memories in parallel, 8 bits at a time); SDR and DTR; data strobe; programmable opcode and frame format; transmit and receive FIFO; 8-, 16- and 32-bit accesses; DMA in indirect mode; interrupts on FIFO threshold, timeout, completion and access error. Under TrustZone the OCTOSPI bank starts secure after reset; at most two nonsecure areas are set through the TZSC MPCWM1 and MPCWM5 in 64-Kbyte steps, and the registers can be made secure through the TZSC.

A full I/O matrix, ahead of the alternate-function map, that assigns the OCTOSPI pins by function (data, control, clock) and multiplexes single, dual, quad and octal SPI interfaces on one bus, for memories sharing a multichip package. Up to two interfaces and two ports.

Makes an output clock phase-shifted from its input clock, at a phase set by the application, used to clock received data in the SDMMC or Octo-SPI. The delay varies with voltage and temperature, so the phase may need re-centring. Input clock 25 to 160 MHz, up to 12 oversampling phases.

A 14-bit successive-approximation ADC with up to 20 multiplexed channels: up to 17 external inputs from GPIO pads and three internal ones, VREFINT, the temperature sensor (VSENSE) and VBAT/4. Resolution 14, 12, 10 or 8 bits, a lower resolution converting faster; conversion time does not depend on the AHB clock. Inputs are single-ended or differential per channel. Self-calibration of offset and linearity, sampling time per channel, up to four injected channels with hardware context preparation, four injected data registers, regular data by GPDMA with a FIFO, and data routed to the MDF. It sits on the AHB bus. An oversampler with a 32-bit register gives ratios from 2 to 1024 with programmable right and left shift; gain and offset compensation precondition the data. For low power: a speed-adaptive mode at low clock, slow bus operation, and an auto-delayed mode that avoids overrun at low AHB clock. Conversions start by software or by hardware triggers of selectable polarity (timer events, GPIO inputs), for regular and injected groups, in single, scan, continuous or discontinuous mode; results are left- or right-aligned in a 32-bit register. Interrupts on ready, end of sampling, end of conversion and of sequence (regular or injected), analog watchdog 1, 2 or 3, and overrun. Three analog watchdogs with filtering of out-of-range data. Input range VSSA < VIN < VREF+. The analog clock must be between 5 MHz and 55 MHz.

A 12-bit successive-approximation ADC with up to 25 multiplexed channels: up to 19 external inputs and six internal ones, the temperature sensor (VSENSE), VREFINT, the core voltage VCORE, the VBAT pin, and two internal DAC channels. Resolution 12, 10, 8 or 6 bits; conversion takes 0.4 µs at 12 bits (2.5 MHz), less at lower resolution. Self-calibration, programmable sampling time, DMA. Low-power features: a reduced HCLK with full ADC performance, wait mode against overrun at low HCLK, auto-off between conversions, and autonomous mode down to Stop 2, in which a trigger switches the ADC on, it converts, stores by DMA to SRAM and switches off; its interrupts wake the part from Stop 0, Stop 1 and Stop 2. Conversions start by software or by hardware triggers of selectable polarity, single or scanned, once per trigger, continuous or discontinuous; results are left- or right-aligned in a 16-bit register. Interrupts on end of sampling, conversion or sequence, analog watchdog and overrun, with wake-up from Stop. Oversampler with a 16-bit register, ratio 2 to 256 and a shift of up to 8 bits. Supply 1.62 to 3.6 V; input range VSSA < VIN < VREF+. The analog clock must be between 140 kHz and 55 MHz.

Produces a voltage VSENSE linear with temperature, wired inside to an input of ADC1 and ADC4. Its offset differs from part to part, so uncalibrated it suits only the detection of temperature changes; each part is calibrated in the factory and the values are kept read-only in system memory.
A bandgap reference for the ADCs and comparators, wired inside to inputs of ADC1 and ADC4. Its exact voltage is measured on each part in production test and kept read-only in system memory.
VBAT can be measured on an ADC1 or ADC4 channel. Because VBAT may exceed VDDA, the pin reaches the ADC through an internal divide-by-four bridge, so the result is a quarter of VBAT.

One 12-bit voltage-output DAC controller driving two output channels with a converter apiece, in 8- or 12-bit mode (12-bit data left or right aligned), with DMA. The two channels convert independently or together with synchronized update. Reference from the VREF+ pin (shared with the other analog blocks) or the internal reference on that pin. An output can be disconnected from its DAC_OUTx pin and routed to on-chip peripherals, leaving the pin free as a GPIO. Optional output buffer for higher drive, per-channel calibration including buffer offset calibration, buffered or unbuffered output. Noise, triangle and sawtooth wave generation, external triggers, DMA per channel with underrun detection and double-data DMA. Sample-and-hold mode for low power in Stop, where the output can be updated by DMA, and an autonomous mode.

A buffer from VREFINT to the VREF+ pin giving 1.5 V, 1.8 V, 2.048 V or 2.5 V as reference for the ADCs, DACs and external parts. With the buffer off, an external reference can be applied to VREF+. On packages where VREF+ is double-bonded with VDDA the buffer is not available.

Two rail-to-rail comparators; reference, hysteresis, output polarity and speed are programmable, the slow setting drawing less power. The reference is an I/O, a DAC output channel, or the internal reference or 1/4, 1/2 or 3/4 of it. They can wake the part from Stop 0, Stop 1 and Stop 2, raise interrupts and timer breaks, and pair as a window comparator.
Two op amps that work as a PGA or as a follower routed inside or outside the chip, with low input bias current, low offset voltage, a low-power mode and rail-to-rail input.

Filters the bitstreams of external sigma-delta modulators, for audio capture, motor control and metering. Six serial interfaces (SPI, Manchester-coded one-wire, or PDM for digital microphones) and six filter paths, joined by a bitstream matrix, two common clock inputs or outputs for the modulators, and two inputs from the internal ADCs. Each path has a CIC filter (splittable into a high-resolution filter and an out-of-limit detector, or set as Sinc4 or Sinc5, with adjustable decimation), a reshape filter, a high-pass filter against DC offset, offset error cancellation, gain control, saturation and an out-of-limit detector with its own thresholds (suited to overcurrent detection). A short-circuit detector with very short latency and its own thresholds is available on each selected bitstream, and a clock absence detector. Output is 16- or 24-bit signed, at up to 24-bit resolution, set by filter type, order, decimation and integrator length; single or continuous conversion; per-bitstream delay; flexible triggers for simultaneous or delayed conversions; breaks on out-of-limit or short-circuit events; autonomous in Stop; DMA to RAM and interrupts. All processing runs on the kernel clock; the AHB clock is requested only to move data or signal an event.

A one-channel subset of the MDF for audio capture and metering: one serial interface (SPI, Manchester, PDM), one filter path (CIC as Sinc4 or Sinc5 with adjustable decimation, reshape filter, high-pass filter, gain control, saturation), a bitstream matrix and two common clock inputs or outputs. Output 16- or 24-bit signed at up to 24-bit resolution, single or continuous conversion, clock absence detector, per-bitstream delay and flexible triggers. A sound activity detector at the filter output, with programmable parameters, keeps samples out of memory until the signal meets the set criteria, cutting power. Autonomous in Stop 0, Stop 1 and Stop 2, where every one of its interrupts wakes the part; DMA and interrupts. Processing runs on the kernel clock; the AHB clock is requested only to move data or signal an event.

A synchronous parallel input for 8-, 10-, 12- or 14-bit CMOS camera modules, with embedded or external line and frame sync, continuous or snapshot capture and cropping. Formats: 8/10/12/14-bit progressive monochrome or raw Bayer, YCbCr 4:2:2, RGB 565 and JPEG. Black-and-white, X24 and X5 cameras are supported; any resizing is done in the camera.

A generic 8- or 16-bit synchronous parallel slave, input or output, with a 4-word (16-byte) FIFO, a data enable input (PSSI_DE) and a ready output (PSSI_RDY) for flow control. It shares its circuitry, alternate functions and interrupt vector with the DCMI, so only one of the two is used at a time and the other's registers cannot be reached.

Capacitive sensing of a finger near an electrode behind glass or plastic by surface charge transfer, supported by the STMTouch library. Up to 22 channels, up to eight acquired in parallel, one sampling capacitor for up to three channels; spread spectrum against noise; hardware-run acquisition with programmable charge-transfer frequency, sampling-capacitor and channel pins; a maximum count to cut short a faulty channel; end-of-acquisition and max-count flags with interrupts. Proximity, touchkey, linear and rotary sensors. The channel count depends on package and free I/Os.

Delivers 32-bit random numbers from an analog entropy source with a NIST SP800-90B approved conditioning stage; it is an SP 800-90B compliant entropy source for building a nondeterministic random bit generator. Four 32-bit samples every 412 AHB clock cycles when fAHB < 77 MHz, otherwise every 256 RNG clock cycles. Start-up and continuous health tests (repetition count, adaptive proportion) with error management. It can be disabled, or run with automatic low-power mode (the default). AHB slave reached by 32-bit word accesses only; any other access gives a bus error and writes are ignored.

SHA-1, SHA-224, SHA-256, MD5 and HMAC, to FIPS PUB 180-4, FIPS PUB 186-4, RFC 1321, RFC 2104 and FIPS PUB 198-1, giving 160-, 224- and 256-bit digests (128-bit for MD5) of messages up to 2^64 - 1 bits. One 512-bit block takes 82 clock cycles in SHA-1, 66 in SHA-256 and 66 in MD5. Automatic padding to 512-bit blocks, bit, byte, half-word and word swapping, a 32-bit input register with a 16-word FIFO, eight 32-bit digest registers H0 to H7, DMA on one channel (single or fixed burst of 4), and suspend/resume of a computation with reloadable digest registers. AHB slave reached by 32-bit word accesses only.
The timer set: TIM1 and TIM8 (advanced control), as many as seven general-purpose timers, TIM6 and TIM7 (basic), LPTIM1 to LPTIM4 (low power), the IWDG and WWDG watchdogs, and two SysTick timers.

Three-phase PWM on six channels with complementary outputs and programmable dead time, or full general-purpose timers. The four independent channels do input capture, output compare, edge- or centre-aligned PWM from 0 to 100 % and one-pulse output. In debug the counter can be frozen and the PWM outputs disabled so power switches turn off. They share the general-purpose timer architecture and link to those timers for synchronization or event chaining.

TIM2 to TIM5: 32-bit auto-reload up/down counter, 16-bit prescaler, four independent channels, each doing capture, compare, PWM or one-pulse output, independent DMA requests and quadrature encoder input. TIM15, TIM16 and TIM17: 16-bit auto-reload up counter and 16-bit prescaler; TIM15 has two channels plus one complementary output, TIM16 and TIM17 one channel plus one complementary output, all usable for capture, compare, PWM or one-pulse, with independent DMA requests. All link for synchronization or event chaining and can be frozen in debug.
16-bit time bases, used mainly to trigger the DAC.

Four timers with their own clock that keep counting in Stop while their clock is HSI16, MSI, LSE, LSI or an external one, and can wake the part from Stop. LPTIM1, LPTIM3 and LPTIM4 run in Stop 0, Stop 1 and Stop 2; LPTIM2 in Stop 0 and Stop 1. 16-bit up counter with 16-bit auto-reload and 16-bit capture/compare registers, 3-bit prescaler (divide by 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64 or 128). Internal clocks LSE, LSI, HSI16, and MSIK (LPTIM1, 3, 4) or the APB clock (LPTIM2), or an external clock on the LPTIM input that needs no low-power oscillator (pulse counting). Continuous or one-shot, software or hardware trigger, programmable glitch filter, pulse or PWM output, configurable polarity, encoder mode, repetition counter, up to two channels for input capture, edge-aligned PWM or one-pulse output, interrupts on 10 events, DMA requests on update and input capture.
Drives an infrared LED for remote control, built from internal connections to TIM16 and TIM17.

12-bit down counter with an 8-bit prescaler, clocked from the 32 kHz LSI independently of the main clock, so it runs in Stop and Standby. Resets the part on a fault or serves as a free-running timeout timer. The option bytes choose hardware or software start, and a debug halt can freeze the counter.
7-bit down counter, can run free, clocked from the main clock; resets the part on a fault, has an early-warning interrupt, and can be frozen in debug.

The Cortex-M33 has two SysTick timers, a secure and a nonsecure instance, when TrustZone is on; with TrustZone off there is one. Each is a 24-bit down counter with auto-reload, a maskable interrupt at zero and a programmable clock source, meant for an RTOS or as a plain counter.

BCD calendar with sub-seconds, seconds, minutes, hours (12 or 24 h), weekday, date, month and year, with automatic month-length and leap year handling, or a binary mode with a 32-bit free-running counter. Two alarms; on-the-fly shift of 1 to 32767 RTC clock pulses to synchronize with a master clock; reference clock input (50 or 60 Hz) for better calendar precision; digital calibration with 0.95 ppm resolution against crystal error; timestamp on the timestamp pin, a tamper event or the switch to VBAT; 17-bit auto-reload wake-up timer. Fully securable, with each of the two alarms, the wake-up timer and the timestamp set secure or nonsecure and privileged or not. Supplied through a switch from VDD when present or else VBAT. Clock: LSE crystal (32.768 kHz) or external resonator or oscillator, LSI (32 kHz typical), or HSE divided in the RCC. Clocked by the LSE it works in VBAT mode and every low-power mode; clocked by the LSI it works in every low-power mode except Shutdown, and not in VBAT mode. Every RTC event (alarm, wake-up timer, timestamp) can interrupt and wake the part from low-power modes.

32 backup registers of 32 bits in the backup domain, kept in every low-power mode and in VBAT mode, guarded with the other secrets by the tamper logic, which can erase the backup registers, backup SRAM, SRAM2, the caches and the HASH. Up to 8 tamper pins: active mode continually compares tamper outputs with inputs to catch opens and shorts, from 4 meshes (each input with its own output) to 7 meshes (one output shared by up to 7 inputs); passive mode detects edges or levels at ultra-low power with internal pull-up handling; digital filter. 11 internal tamper events: backup domain voltage, temperature, LSE, RTC calendar overflow, JTAG/SWD access with RDP not 0, monotonic counter overflow, RNG fault, IWDG reset with a tamper flag already set, and 3 ADC4 watchdogs. Each tamper erases secrets at once in hardware mode (backup registers included) or on software command in software mode; any tamper can make an RTC timestamp. TrustZone: each tamper secure or nonsecure; backup registers in three areas of configurable size, read/write secure, write secure and read nonsecure, and read/write nonsecure; privilege protection of the tamper settings and backup registers. A monotonic counter is included.

Four I2C interfaces handling the bus sequencing, protocol, arbitration and timing. Compatible with I2C-bus specification rev. 5: slave and master, multimaster, Standard-mode up to 100 Kbit/s, Fast-mode up to 400 Kbit/s, Fast-mode Plus up to 1 Mbit/s with 20 mA output drive, 7- and 10-bit addressing with several 7-bit own addresses, programmable setup and hold, and clock stretching that can be turned off. SMBus rev 3.0 (hardware PEC with ACK control, ARP, SMBus alert) and PMBus rev 1.3. An independent kernel clock keeps the bit rate unaffected by PCLK changes. Autonomous in Stop with wake-up, analog and digital noise filters (programmable), and a one-byte buffer served by DMA.
Three USARTs (USART1 to USART3), two UARTs (UART4, UART5) and one LPUART (LPUART1).

Full-duplex asynchronous NRZ communication with a fractional baud-rate generator; up to 20 Mbaud using DMA with several buffers. Oversampling by 16 or 8, transmit and receive FIFOs that can each be enabled with status flags, one programmable baud rate for both directions, a kernel clock independent of PCLK, auto baud-rate detection, 7-, 8- or 9-bit words, MSB or LSB first, 1 or 2 stop bits. Synchronous master or slave with clock output or input, SPI slave underrun flag, single-wire half duplex, continuous DMA to or from SRAM, separate transmitter and receiver enables, separate polarity control, swappable TX/RX pins, hardware flow control for modems and RS-485 transceivers, error flags, parity generation and checking, interrupts, multiprocessor wake-up from mute by idle line or address mark, and autonomous operation in Stop with wake-up. LIN: 13-bit break generation and 10/11-bit break detection. IrDA SIR with 3/16-bit pulses in normal mode. Smartcard T = 0 and T = 1 to ISO/IEC 7816-3 with 0.5 and 1.5 stop bits. Modbus with timeout and CR/LF recognition.

Asynchronous serial at minimum power: with only the 32.768 kHz LSE it runs from 300 to 9600 baud, so it can wait for a frame in Stop; a faster clock gives higher baud rates. Full duplex NRZ, half-duplex single wire, CTS/RTS modem control and RS-485 flow control, multiprocessor mode, transmit and receive FIFOs with status flags, kernel clock independent of PCLK, 7-, 8- or 9-bit words, MSB or LSB first, 1 or 2 stop bits, DMA, separate enables and polarity control, swappable TX/RX, flags for a full receive buffer, an empty transmit buffer, busy and transmission complete, parity, overrun, noise, frame and parity error flags, interrupts, wake-up from mute by idle line or address mark, and autonomous operation in Stop with wake-up.

Three SPIs, master or slave, multimaster or multislave, full duplex on three lines, half duplex on two (bidirectional data line) or simplex on two. The master supplies SCK; optional SS and RDY signals select a slave and pace the data. Motorola format by default and TI format. Data size 4 to 32 bits (or 8 and 16 bits only on the limited instance); kernel clock separate from PCLK; a baud-rate prescaler reaching kernel clock/2, or the RCC clock directly in master mode; protected configuration; hardware or software SS for master and slave with configurable polarity and timing and programmable minimum delays; MISO/MOSI swap; programmable clock polarity and phase; MSB or LSB first; a programmable number of data per transaction controlling SS and CRC; hardware CRC appended on transmit and checked on receive; interrupts on overrun, CRC error, slave underrun and master mode fault; two embedded receive and transmit FIFOs (16 x or 8 x 8-bit) with DMA and configurable thresholds; configurable behaviour on slave underrun for cascaded circular buffers; autonomous operation in Stop with wake-up; optional RDY status pin.

Two SAIs, each with two independent audio sub-blocks that transmit or receive, each with an 8-word FIFO, synchronous or asynchronous to each other, master or slave independently, with a clock generator per block for independent sample rates when both are masters. Data size 8, 10, 16, 20, 24 or 32 bits; protocols such as I2S, PCM/DSP, TDM, AC'97, SPDIF out and MSB- or LSB-justified; as many as 16 slots of configurable size with selectable active slots; configurable bits per frame, frame-sync level, offset and length, first-bit position, LSB or MSB first, strobing edge; mute; stereo or mono. Error flags with interrupts for overrun and underrun, early or late frame sync in slave mode and codec not ready in AC'97 receive; interrupts on errors and FIFO requests; two DMA channels, one per sub-block FIFO.

Host controller on the AHB bus for e•MMC devices, SDIO cards and SD memory cards. e•MMC 5.1 with 1-bit (default), 4-bit and 8-bit buses (HS200 with SDMMC_CK limited to the highest allowed I/O speed; HS400 not supported), backward compatible with earlier MMC. SD memory card 6.0 and SDIO 4.0, 1-bit (default) and 4-bit (SDR104 with SDMMC_CK limited to the highest allowed I/O speed; no SPI mode, no UHS-II). Up to 208 Mbyte/s in 8-bit mode, depending on the allowed I/O speed. Output-enable signals for data and command to drive external bidirectional buffers; IDMA with linked lists. One SD/SDIO/e•MMC card at a time, or a stack of e•MMC.

With both SDMMCs in use only one can run e•MMC with an 8-bit bus. The SDMMC1 SDIO voltage switch and an 8-bit e•MMC on SDMMC2 exclude each other: if SDMMC1 needs SDIO UHS-I modes (SDR12, SDR25, SDR50, SDR104 or DDR50), SDMMC2 cannot run 8-bit e•MMC; if SDMMC2 runs 8-bit e•MMC, SDMMC1 supports only SDIO default and high-speed modes.

One CAN module with a shared message RAM and a configuration block, conforming to ISO 11898-1:2015 (CAN 2.0 A and B) and -4, and CAN FD 1.0 with up to 64 data bytes. A 0.8-Kbyte message RAM holds the filters, two receive FIFOs, each of three payloads of up to 64 bytes, the transmit event FIFO and a transmit FIFO or queue of three payloads. Error logging, support for AUTOSAR and J1939, improved acceptance filters, separate signalling of high-priority messages received, loop-back test mode, maskable interrupts, separate APB and CAN kernel clock domains, power-down support.

Device, host or OTG controller with an on-chip full-speed PHY, USB-IF certified to USB 2.0 and to OTG 2.0, with software-configured endpoints and suspend/resume. It needs an exact 48 MHz clock, from the PLL (with an HSE crystal as source) or from HSI48 auto-trimmed to the USB SOF, which allows crystal-less operation. OTG: A/B identification on ID, HNP and SRP, VBUS switch-off by the host, VBUS level monitoring by internal comparators, dynamic role change; it runs as an SRP-capable FS device, an SRP-capable FS/LS host or a dual-role device. SOF pulse to a pad or internally to a timer, configurable frame period and end-of-frame interrupt; LPM; power saving by system stop during suspend and gating of internal clocks, PHY and FIFO power. 1.25 Kbytes of dedicated RAM partitioned into FIFOs whose sizes need not be powers of two, each holding several packets. Guaranteed bandwidth for up to one 1 ms frame without system intervention. Battery Charging 1.2 charging port detection on the FS PHY. Host: external charge pump for VBUS, up to 12 reconfigurable channels, a hardware scheduler with up to 12 periodic (interrupt and isochronous) and 12 non-periodic (control and bulk) requests, shared receive FIFO and periodic and non-periodic transmit FIFOs. Device: one bidirectional control endpoint 0, 5 IN and 5 OUT endpoints (bulk, interrupt or isochronous), a shared receive FIFO and transmit-OUT FIFO, up to 6 dedicated transmit-IN FIFOs, soft disconnect.

operation.topic: USB Type-C and Power Delivery controller (UCPD)
operation.text: One controller for USB Power Delivery Rev. 3.0 and for Type-C as defined in release 2.0 of the cable and connector specification, on dedicated I/Os that carry the Type-C Rp pull-ups (every value) and Rd pull-downs and support a dead battery, with PD message transmit and receive, and fast role swap (FRS). The digital part does Type-C level detection with debounce and interrupts, FRS detection with interrupt, a byte-level PD payload interface with interrupts and DMA, PD timing dividers with a clock prescaler, CRC generation and checking, 4b5b coding, ordered sets with a programmable receive mask, and frequency recovery during the preamble. It runs at low power in Stop and still detects incoming PD messages and FRS signalling.

The SWJ-DP combines JTAG and serial-wire debug ports. Serial-wire debug uses two pins instead of the five of JTAG: TMS is shared with SWDIO and TCK with SWCLK, and a set sequence on TMS switches between JTAG-DP and SW-DP; unused JTAG pins can serve as GPIOs. The Arm ETM streams compressed instruction and data trace at a high rate over a few ETM pins to an external trace port analyzer, for display by third-party debugger software.

Every package but WLCSP90 has two pinouts. The SMPS pinout (ordering suffix Q) has VLXSMPS, VDDSMPS, VSSSMPS and VDD11 for the step-down converter; the pinout without SMPS has VCAP and gives more GPIOs, wake-up pins, tamper pins and ADC channels on most packages. WLCSP90 has the SMPS pinout only. LQFP144 has 114 GPIOs without SMPS and 111 with it.

Every voltage is measured from VSS unless stated. Min and max figures hold over the full range of ambient temperature, supply and frequency; every part is tested at TA = 25 °C and at TA max of its temperature range. Figures a table note marks as from characterization, simulation or design are not production tested; a characterized min or max is the sample mean ±3σ. Typical figures are for TA = 25 °C and VDD = VDDA = 3 V, as guidance only and untested; typical ADC accuracy is the figure 95 % of a standard-lot sample meet over the full temperature and supply range (mean ±2σ). Typical curves are guidance only. A pin parameter is measured with 50 pF from the pin to ground, and a pin's input voltage is taken between the pin and VSS.

Each supply pair (VDD/VSS, VDDA/VSSA and the rest) takes ceramic decoupling capacitors at its pins, on the board right next to them or under them on the far side. Without SMPS: each VDD pin 100 nF plus one 10 µF for the group, each VDDIO2 pin 100 nF plus one 4.7 µF, VDDA 100 nF + 1 µF, VREF+ 100 nF + 1 µF, VDDUSB 100 nF, and VCAP 4.7 µF. The VCAP capacitor is 4.7 µF or 2 × 2.2 µF ±20 %, ESR under 20 mΩ at 3 MHz, rated 10 V or more; the UFBGA169 has two VCAP balls and each takes a 2.2 µF (typical) capacitor.

On the SMPS parts (xQ order codes) the SMPS and the LDO both can supply VCORE, one at a time. With the SMPS running, its VLXSMPS output is filtered by the inductor and drives the two VDD11 pins; with the LDO running, the LDO regulates VCORE on the same VDD11 capacitors. A 100 nF capacitor at each VDD11 pin is advised but optional. VDD11 capacitors: 2 × 2.2 µF ±20 %, ESR under 20 mΩ at 3 MHz, rated 10 V or more. VDDSMPS input capacitor: 10 µF ±20 %, ESR under 10 mΩ at 3 MHz, rated 10 V or more. Inductor from VLXSMPS to VDD11: 2.2 µH ±20 %, saturation current above 0.5 A, DC resistance under 200 mΩ.
Every IDD figure is the total current of the part: the sum drawn on VDD, VDDIO2, VDDA, VDDUSB, VBAT and, on SMPS parts, VDDSMPS.

Stress above the ratings of the voltage, current and thermal tables can damage the part for good; they are stress limits, with no operation implied there, and long exposure at them may reduce reliability. The mission profile is qualified to JEDEC JESD47; longer mission profiles are available on request.

Supply current depends on supply voltage, temperature, pin loading, software configuration, clock frequencies, I/O switching, where the code runs from and the code itself. For the typical and maximum figures every I/O is an analog input, every peripheral is off unless a table says otherwise, flash runs with the fewest wait states for fHCLK (wait-state tables in the reference manual), fPCLK = fHCLK when peripherals are on, and the voltage range follows fHCLK: range 1 for 110 MHz < fHCLK ≤ 160 MHz, range 2 for 55 MHz < fHCLK ≤ 110 MHz, range 3 for 25 MHz < fHCLK ≤ 55 MHz, range 4 for fHCLK ≤ 25 MHz. Temperature and supply are within the general operating conditions.

An input with pull-up or pull-down draws current whenever the pin is held at the opposite level; the pull resistor values give the figure. Outputs add any internal or external pull and the load. An input sitting at an intermediate voltage draws current through its Schmitt trigger; configuring such pins as analog avoids it, and ADC inputs are configured as analog. A floating input can drift to an intermediate level or toggle from noise, so unused pins are set to analog mode or held at a defined level by a pull resistor or by output mode.

A switching I/O draws current from its I/O supply to drive the pin circuit and to charge and discharge the internal and external load capacitance, on top of the peripheral currents. It is measured with the pin a push-pull output toggled by software at a fixed rate.

Each peripheral's dynamic figure is the difference in supply current between the peripheral clocked and not clocked, with every I/O in analog mode and temperature and supply within the general operating conditions. It covers the digital part only; the analog part of a peripheral is given in that peripheral's own section.
A wake-up time runs from the wake-up event to the first user instruction executed, with FSTEN = 1 in PWR_CR3 unless stated; the part enters the low-power mode through a WFE instruction.

In bypass mode the HSE or LSE oscillator is off and its input pin is an ordinary GPIO; the external clock meets the I/O characteristics. The HSE input takes a digital square wave (HSEEXT = 1, 30 %/70 % thresholds of VDD) or an analog signal (HSEEXT = 0, rise and fall measured 10 % to 90 %); the LSE input takes a square or a sine wave.

The HSE oscillator runs from a 4 MHz to 48 MHz crystal or ceramic resonator; its figures come from design simulation with typical external parts. The resonator and its load capacitors go as near the oscillator pins as possible, to keep output distortion and start-up settling low. Crystal selection is covered in application note AN2867.

The LSE oscillator runs from a 32.768 kHz crystal; its figures come from design simulation with typical external parts. Crystal and load capacitors go as near the oscillator pins as possible. CL1 and CL2 are the external load capacitors; the stray capacitance CS is the pins' internal parasitic capacitance (CS_PARA) plus the board's. No resistor may be fitted between OSC32_IN and OSC32_OUT. Crystal selection is covered in application note AN2867.

Susceptibility is tested on samples during characterization. A simple program toggling two LEDs runs while the part is stressed until it fails: ESD (positive and negative) on every pin to IEC 61000-4-2, and fast transient bursts (positive and negative) on VDD and VSS through 100 pF to IEC 61000-4-4. A reset brings the part back to normal operation. Levels and classes follow application note AN1709.

EMC is characterized at component level with a typical setup and simple software; the result in an application depends heavily on that application's software, so EMC software optimization and pre-qualification tests are advised. The software handles runaway conditions: a corrupted program counter, an unexpected reset, corrupted control registers. Most such faults can be reproduced by holding NRST or the oscillator pins low for 1 s, and by ESD stress on the part within its specified range; AN1015 covers software techniques against them.
Emission is monitored with a simple program toggling two LEDs, to IEC 61967-2, which sets the test board and pin loading.

ESD: a positive then a negative pulse 1 s apart on the pins of each sample, for every pin combination, on 3 × (n + 1) samples where n is the number of supply pins, to the ANSI/JEDEC standard. Latch-up: on three parts, an overvoltage on each supply pin and a current injection into every I/O and control pin, to EIA/JESD78E.

Current into an I/O pin from a voltage below VSS or above VDDIOx is avoided in normal operation. Its robustness is checked on samples: current is injected into one floating-input pin at a time while a simple program runs, and a failure is a parameter out of range: an ADC error above 5 LSB TUE, induced leakage on neighbouring pins outside -5 µA to +0 µA, a reset, or an oscillator frequency shift. Negative injection causes negative induced leakage, positive injection positive.

Every I/O is CMOS- and TTL-compliant with no software setting, and its thresholds cover more than the strict CMOS or TTL levels. VIL max is tested in production at 0.3 × VDDIOx and by simulation reaches 0.38 × VDDIOx; VIH min is tested at 0.7 × VDDIOx and by simulation is 0.5 × VDDIOx + 0.2 V; TTL asks for VIL ≤ 0.8 V and VIH ≥ 2 V.

GPIOs other than PC13, PC14 and PC15 sink or source up to ±8 mA, and up to ±20 mA with relaxed VOL/VOH. PC13, PC14 and PC15 share +3 mA of source current between them and sink as much as the other GPIOs. The current sourced by all I/Os on VDDIOx plus the part's own maximum current on VDD stays within ΣIVDD, and the current sunk by all I/Os plus the part's own current on VSS within ΣIVSS (current ratings).

Rise and fall times run between 10 % and 90 % of the output swing. The maximum frequency is reached with a 45 % to 55 % duty cycle into the specified load capacitance. The speed is set by the OSPEEDRy[1:0] bits (reference manual).

The NRST input is CMOS, with a permanent pull-up RPU to VDD, a Schmitt trigger and a filter ahead of the internal reset. An external 0.1 µF capacitor from NRST to ground, placed as close to the part as possible, guards against stray resets, and a push-button to ground may sit beside it. Whatever drives NRST must take it below VIL(NRST) max, or the reset is missed.
An interrupt input pulse is guaranteed to reach the event controller only if it is at least PLEC long.

The ADC1 figures hold over the general operating conditions of ambient temperature, fHCLK and VDDA. A calibration run after every power-up is advised. Below VDDA = 2.4 V the booster on the analog I/O switches is turned on (BOOSTEN = 1 in SYSCFG_CFGR1); from 2.4 V up it is off. On some packages VREF+ is bonded to VDDA and VREF- to VSSA inside the part.

With n bits of resolution one LSB is VREF+/2^n (VDDA/2^n where VREF+ is tied to VDDA). ET, total unadjusted error, is the largest gap between the real and the ideal transfer curve. EO, offset error, is the gap between the first real code transition and the first ideal one. EG, gain error, is the gap between the last ideal transition and the last real one. ED, differential linearity error, is the largest departure of a real code step from the ideal step. EL, integral linearity error, is the largest departure of any real transition from the straight line joining the end points.

A source VAIN with resistance RAIN feeds an ADC input through the pin's analog switch into the sampling switch, the sampling resistance RADC and the hold capacitor CADC. The pin carries a parasitic capacitance (board plus pad, the pad's own figure in the I/O static characteristics) and the I/O leakage Ilkg. A large parasitic capacitance costs accuracy; lowering fADC wins it back. Supplies are decoupled as the power supply scheme shows, with a good ceramic 100 nF next to the chip.

The ADC4 figures hold over the general operating conditions of ambient temperature, fHCLK and VDDA, and a calibration after every power-up is advised. Its error terms, input connection and board advice are the same as for ADC1.

Each 12-bit DAC channel drives DAC_OUTx through an output buffer that lowers the output impedance so an external load can be driven with no op-amp; the BOFFx bit in DAC_CR bypasses it. The specified load is RLOAD and CLOAD from the output to ground.

operation.topic: Temperature and backup domain supply monitoring
operation.text: The thresholds of the temperature and backup-domain supply monitors are given in technical note TN1333 for PCI products, available under NDA.
In synchronous mode FMC_CLK runs at up to 80 MHz with CL = 15 pF or 20 pF, both for 2.7 V ≤ VDD ≤ 3.6 V and for 1.71 V ≤ VDD ≤ 1.9 V.

Configured as the reference manual sets out, the I2C interfaces meet the timing of the I2C-bus specification rev. 03 in Standard-mode (to 100 kbit/s), Fast-mode (to 400 kbit/s) and Fast-mode Plus (to 1 Mbit/s); this is set by design and not tested in production. SDA and SCL are not true open-drain pins: in open-drain mode the PMOS to VDDIOx is switched off but still there. Only FT_f pins meet the Fm+ low-level output current. Every SDA and SCL pin has an analog spike filter.
The UCPD controller conforms to revision 1.2 of the USB Type-C specification and revision 3.0 of USB Power Delivery.

The top side carries the product identification (for example STM32U575 with the order-code suffix), a date code of year and week, a revision code and the pin 1 or ball A1 mark; marking varies with the supply chain, and other optional marks may appear. Parts marked ES or E, or shipped with an engineering-sample notice, are not qualified and not for production use.
The thermal resistances are taken by JESD51-2 (natural convection, still air). ST application note AN5036 covers thermal management of STM32 applications.
